evidence.intro: Does the stress signal agree with what satellites saw on this field? Each year, modelled water stress is compared with how green the vegetation was against its own average.

evidence.baseline.body: The engine did not provide a back-test for this request, so this page shows the contract fixture: the engine's back-test for the demo field (37.89° N, 28.98° E) as published in docs/VALIDATION.md. It is not computed for the field you selected.
evidence.r.title: Correlation
evidence.r.negative: Negative: in years with more modelled stress, the vegetation was usually less green than its average. That is the direction a useful stress signal should show.
evidence.r.positive: Positive: in years with more modelled stress, the vegetation was usually greener than its average. That is the opposite of what a useful stress signal should show.
evidence.r.zero: Zero: no linear relationship between modelled stress and vegetation in these years.
evidence.r.scale: r runs from −1 to 1. Values near 0 mean little linear relationship; values near −1 or 1 mean the two series move closely together.

landing.problem.title: The problem
landing.problem.body: Farms in dry regions such as the Büyük Menderes basin face hotter and more variable growing seasons. Which crops to grow, and in what order, decides how much water a field needs and how often it runs short. Long climate and satellite records exist for every field on Earth, but they are rarely turned into an answer for one specific field.

landing.limits.title: What it cannot tell you
landing.limits.grid: Weather is an average over a grid cell of about 55 × 55 km, not a measurement in your field.
landing.limits.soil: Soil values are model predictions for a 250 m pixel with wide uncertainty; your own soil test is better.
landing.limits.pixel: The vegetation check uses one 250 m pixel whose land use is unknown, and so far one site.
landing.limits.past: Every number is replayed from past weather. Travertine makes no forecast of future climate.
landing.limits.yield: Scores compare rotations with each other; they are not yield or price forecasts.
landing.team.title: Team
landing.ai: Built with AI coding tools under human review: Claude Code (Anthropic) agents for the engine, contract and web app, and OpenAI Codex, which a teammate used to build the current interface and the Cosmo guide. Humans review every change before it is merged. Cosmo answers questions with Google Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash-lite), told to use only the engine's data for the selected field; each such answer is labelled, and without Gemini Cosmo falls back to fixed, reviewed texts. The full statement is in docs/AI_USE.md.

cosmo.tour.0.title: Hello, I'm Cosmo!
cosmo.tour.0.text: Welcome to Travertine. I'll show you where the real field data and the rotation suggestions are.
cosmo.tour.1.title: Overview
cosmo.tour.1.text: Here you see the selected field's climate, soil and water at a glance. Watch for the demo field label.
cosmo.tour.2.title: Climate record
cosmo.tour.2.text: This is not today's weather: it is the mean temperature over the years on record at this location. The badge shows whether it comes from the live engine or demo data.
cosmo.tour.3.title: Soil and vegetation
cosmo.tour.3.text: NDVI summarises vegetation; next to it are soil texture and pH. The detailed analysis is on the field screen.
cosmo.tour.4.title: Water balance
cosmo.tour.4.text: Compare yearly rainfall with the evaporative demand that tells how much water crops need.
cosmo.tour.5.title: Field view
cosmo.tour.5.text: The values here come from the selected field's analysis. Open the map to change the location.
cosmo.tour.6.title: Field
cosmo.tour.6.text: Now I'll click here and show you how to choose a field on the map.
cosmo.tour.7.title: Map
cosmo.tour.7.text: Search for a place, drop a point or draw the field boundary. The location is kept in the address bar and can be shared.
cosmo.tour.8.title: Let's pick the demo field
cosmo.tour.8.text: Cosmo is selecting the demo location now. You can change to your own field from the same place later.
cosmo.tour.9.title: Field summary
cosmo.tour.9.text: Climate record, soil properties and vegetation are shown here with their data sources.
cosmo.tour.10.title: Rotations
cosmo.tour.10.text: This page ranks crop sequences over several years and shows each option's scores.
cosmo.tour.11.title: Your priorities
cosmo.tour.11.text: When you move the water, income, soil-health and risk sliders, the ranking is recalculated.
cosmo.tour.12.title: Ranked options
cosmo.tour.12.text: Each card shows crops by year, scores and water need. You can compare two options side by side.
cosmo.tour.13.title: Evidence
cosmo.tour.13.text: Now I'll show you which past records the results were checked against.
cosmo.tour.14.title: Model check
cosmo.tour.14.text: The chart compares modelled water stress with the vegetation satellites saw, year by year.
cosmo.tour.15.title: Method and limits
cosmo.tour.15.text: Data resolution, model assumptions and uncertainty are written out here. Read these limits before deciding.
cosmo.tour.16.title: Tour complete
cosmo.tour.16.text: We've visited the main sections. Ask Cosmo about the screen you're on, or restart the tour any time.

cosmo.gloss.et: Evapotranspiration is the water that leaves a field as vapour: evaporation from the soil plus transpiration through crop leaves. Reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) is the rate for a standard, well-watered grass, computed here with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation from NASA POWER weather. A crop's need is ET₀ multiplied by its crop coefficient (Kc).
cosmo.gloss.smAnomaly: A soil-moisture anomaly is how much wetter or drier the soil is than usual for that place and time of year, measured against the long-term average. Travertine does not compute soil-moisture anomalies yet. It shows NASA POWER root-zone wetness (0 dry, 1 saturated), a modelled value for a grid cell of about 55 × 55 km, not a probe reading from your field.
cosmo.gloss.ndvi: NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index) compares the near-infrared and red light a surface reflects: (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red). Green, dense vegetation gives high values; bare soil gives low values. Travertine uses MODIS NDVI at 250 m and, where the engine provides it, 30 m HLS NDVI.
cosmo.gloss.frost: Frost risk is the chance that the temperature falls to 0 °C or below while a crop is sensitive, for example at flowering. It is judged from daily minimum temperatures on record. On the field page Travertine shows, from NASA POWER, the median last spring and first autumn frost, the frost-free season and the number of frost days; the plan page shows the share of frost days in each month a crop is in the field. These are past frequencies for a grid cell about 50 km across, not a forecast for your field.
cosmo.gloss.waterBalance: A water balance tracks the water in the root zone day by day: rain and irrigation add water, crop evapotranspiration removes it, and water beyond what the soil can hold drains away. When stored water runs low the crop is stressed. Travertine's rotation scores come from this FAO-56 daily balance replayed over past seasons.
cosmo.gloss.satellite: Satellites and models give averages over an area, not a point: a 250 m pixel for MODIS NDVI and a grid cell of about 55 × 55 km for NASA POWER weather. A ground station or soil probe measures one spot precisely. Satellite and model data cover every field and many years; ground measurements are more exact where they are taken. Your own field records are better where you have them.
cosmo.r.sleep: I'm resting. Say wake up when you need me.
cosmo.r.ranking: The ranking combines the water, income, soil-health and risk scores with the weights you choose. The scores are not yield forecasts; they are for comparing options.
cosmo.r.data: Each card names the source of its climate, soil and vegetation values, and the Data page lists them all. The badge at the top says whether values come from the live engine or demo data.
cosmo.r.trust: The comparison with past years shows an association, not cause and effect, and it does not guarantee future yields. The correlation, its uncertainty interval and the assumptions are on the Evidence page.
cosmo.r.field: On the field screen, search for a place, drop a point or draw the boundary. The values themselves are shown in the field summary; I do not read them out.
cosmo.r.whoami: I am a guide with fixed, reviewed answers. I have no language model and I do not generate text. Check the badge at the top to see where the data comes from.
cosmo.r.voice: If your browser supports it, ask with the microphone button. You can turn spoken answers on or off in the chat header.

cosmo.r.unknown: I don't have a prepared answer for that. Ask about this screen, choosing a field, the rotations, or a term such as NDVI or evapotranspiration.

landing.challenge.title: How Travertine answers the challenge
landing.challenge.data.q: Use NASA and other Earth observation data
landing.challenge.data.a: Daily NASA POWER weather since 2001, MODIS NDVI at 250 m and HLS at 30 m (when the engine serves it), SoilGrids soil, with provenance on every number.
landing.challenge.local.q: Local soil information and crop characteristics
landing.challenge.local.a: SoilGrids texture, organic carbon, pH and available water for the field; crop coefficients cited from FAO-56 for every crop.
landing.challenge.priorities.a: Four priority sliders (water, income, soil health, risk) re-rank the strategies; the current rotation can be entered as a baseline.
landing.challenge.strategies.a: Every valid 3- to 5-year rotation is replayed through a daily FAO-56 water balance over past seasons and ranked.
landing.challenge.explain.a: Each strategy carries the engine's own explanations and, when the engine provides them, five parts: why suggested, evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks for local review.
landing.challenge.limits.a: A pre-registered back-test against satellite vegetation with confidence intervals, a simple baseline to beat, and caveats shown as returned.
landing.cosmo.title: Meet Cosmo, the guide
landing.cosmo.body: Cosmo walks you through the screens and explains the terms Travertine uses. It answers only from fixed, reviewed text: no language model, no generated advice. Open it from the button at the bottom right.
landing.supports: Travertine supports farmer judgment and local expertise; it does not replace them. Check its suggestions with people who know the field.
landing.roadmap.title: Roadmap
landing.roadmap.plan: Climate trend tests (Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope) and a season-so-far view.
landing.roadmap.scenarios: Outcome ranges (P10, P50, P90) per rotation and the Pareto set: rotations that no other rotation outscores on every objective.
landing.roadmap.hazards: Yield response with published Ky factors (FAO-33, FAO-66).
landing.roadmap.inputs: Field-scale vegetation back to 2013 and IMERG rainfall, which need a NASA Earthdata login.
landing.roadmap.trends: A load test and one command that regenerates every result and figure in the docs.
